tasks.short: Update the syllabus, write homework assignments, prepare handouts, check the materials, and publish them in the learning environment.

steps.what: Lecturer updates the syllabus with dates, readings and learning outcomes
Lecturer writes homework assignments

loop.input: The learning outcomes, the reading list and last year's assignments.
loop.output: Draft assignment variants with instructions and a rubric.
loop.check: Code checks each assignment maps to a learning outcome code and every reading it cites is on the reading list; the lecturer works each assignment through, checks that it fits the outcome and level, and edits and approves it.
loop.stop: One draft per assignment; if it fails the check twice, the lecturer writes it.
loop.why_not_simpler: Assignments must be new each year to limit copying; a fixed bank wears out.

steps.what: Lecturer prepares course materials such as handouts
Lecturer checks the final course materials: assignments fit the outcomes, readings are on the list and handouts are current
Lecturer publishes the checked materials in the learning environment

tasks.design: The syllabus is generated from the course catalogue entry, the timetable and the reading list, so dates and outcomes are not retyped each year. A bounded step on the university's own platform drafts assignment variants from the learning outcomes and earlier assignments; code checks each maps to an outcome and cites only listed readings, and the lecturer edits. Handouts come from the lecturer's library of earlier material. Once checked, the lecturer publishes the materials to the course in the learning environment ({LMS}).
tasks.previous_blocker: Syllabi were retyped each year and assignments written from scratch.
tasks.enabler_now: University chat platforms draft text; catalogue data can fill syllabus templates.
tasks.still_hard: Students can paste assignments into chatbots.
tasks.human_edge: Designing an assignment that makes students think rather than copy.
tasks.altitude: The lecturer edits drafts instead of writing everything.

reach.learn: Whether materials are online before the course starts.

evidence.claim: EduGenAI is a university chat platform in pilot; Utrecht forbids automated grading on it.
Drafting course materials is not an Annex III use; evaluating learning outcomes is.

assumptions: Boundary: from the course plan to materials published; teaching is outside.
Input contract: catalogue entry and reading list current; fallback is retyping.

s1 keeps 40 for checking the generated syllabus; s2 keeps 70 because drafts give variants but the lecturer works through and edits each; s3 keeps 80 because earlier handouts are reused but updated by hand; s5 keeps 20 for publishing.
research_questions: How much drafted text does the lecturer keep?

incremental.description: Lecturer keeps learning outcome codes in the catalogue current.

approvals.approved_version: The syllabus, assignments and handouts exactly as checked by the lecturer in s4, published once to the course in the learning environment; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: drafted assignments need much rework (s2 85) and the catalogue entry is out of date (s1 70) (21.2); high: drafts and catalogue as assumed (34.0).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Search the literature, design and conduct research, analyse data, write the manuscript, format references, check the manuscript with co-authors, and submit it.

steps.what: Lecturer searches the literature
Lecturer designs and conducts research in a particular field of knowledge
Lecturer analyses the data in spreadsheets
Lecturer writes the manuscript to publish findings in professional journals
Lecturer formats references to the journal style
Lecturer checks the final manuscript with co-authors: results, claims and references are right
Lecturer submits the manuscript on the journal's portal

tasks.design: Literature search starts from topic summaries and foundational papers in the citation database, which the lecturer then reads, instead of keyword searching from scratch. The analysis runs as a versioned script on the study data. A reference manager formats citations and checks each resolves to a DOI. Research design, writing and submission stay with the lecturer; no model writes the manuscript.
tasks.previous_blocker: Literature was searched by keyword and references formatted by hand.
tasks.enabler_now: Citation databases give topic summaries; reference managers format and check DOIs.
tasks.still_hard: Summaries miss work outside the database.
tasks.human_edge: Framing a question that matters to teachers in schools.
tasks.altitude: Less searching and formatting; research stays.

reach.learn: Whether drafts arrive with checked references.

evidence.claim: Scopus AI gives topic summaries and foundational papers.
Invented references pass plagiarism checks unflagged.

assumptions: Boundary: from the research question to the manuscript submitted; peer review is outside.
Input contract: database licence held by the university; fallback is keyword search.
research_questions: Does the literature search take fewer hours?

approvals.approved_version: The manuscript exactly as checked with the co-authors in s6, submitted once on the named journal's portal; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: topic summaries add little in this field, so s1 keeps 85 (12.7); high: summaries, script and reference manager as assumed (16.5).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Compile the exam from the item bank, administer it, mark closed questions, grade open answers, set final grades, and publish them to students.

steps.what: Lecturer compiles examinations from earlier questions
Lecturer administers the examination
Lecturer marks closed questions: by hand today; after the change code marks them and the lecturer checks flagged items
Lecturer grades open answers

loop.input: Students' open answers and the rubric.
loop.output: Groups of similar answers with a proposed rubric score per group.
loop.check: Similar answers are grouped but no score is proposed; the examiner reads and grades every answer and double-marks a random sample; agreement is computed by code, and a batch with high disagreement is regraded by hand.
loop.stop: If disagreement on the sample is high, the whole batch is graded by hand.
loop.why_not_simpler: Open answers vary in wording; string matching cannot group them.

steps.what: Lecturer checks and sets the final grades: each grade matches the marks and the grading rules
Lecturer enters grades in the learning environment and the student records system

tasks.design: Exams are built from an item bank tagged by learning outcome, with item statistics from earlier years, following a test blueprint. Closed questions are marked by code. For open answers, similar answers are grouped and no score is proposed; the examiner grades every answer and double-marks a sample, and a batch with high disagreement is graded by hand. The examiner sets the final grades; once set, they go from the learning environment ({LMS}) to the student records system in one step instead of double entry.
tasks.previous_blocker: Exams were assembled by hand, closed questions marked by hand and grades entered twice.
tasks.enabler_now: Item banks, auto-marking and answer grouping are available in university assessment tools.
tasks.still_hard: Generative AI threatens the validity of take-home tests.
tasks.human_edge: Recognising an original answer that the rubric did not foresee.
tasks.altitude: The examiner confirms grouped grades instead of marking every script.

reach.learn: Whether item statistics are used to improve exams.

evidence.claim: Gradescope groups similar answers so each group is graded once.
In four US political science classes, 88% of 3,080 short answers were graded with GPT-4 help with no significant grade difference from human grading.
Examiners appointed by the examination board set results; AI used to evaluate learning outcomes is high-risk under Annex III.

assumptions: Boundary: from the exam plan to grades published; resits and appeals are outside.
Input contract: item bank tagged by outcome; fallback is assembling by hand.
No model proposes or sets a grade; the examiner grades every answer. s3 keeps 10 for flagged items; s4 keeps 70 because grouping saves repeated judgement only.
A DPIA comes before grouping student answers.
s6 is part of keeping grade records, which sibling task 25-1081.00:6157 covers; its saving is counted there, so s6 keeps its full time here.
research_questions: What agreement does the sample double-marking show?

already_counted.description: Lecturer grades grouped answers and double-marks a sample.

incremental.description: Lecturer tags new items by learning outcome.

approvals.approved_version: The final grade per student exactly as checked and set by the examiner in s5, published once from the learning environment to the student records system; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: grouping helps little on essay answers (s4 90) and the item bank is thin (s1 80) (20.5); high: grouping and item bank as assumed (33.5).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Scan journals and newsletters, read current literature, talk with colleagues, attend conferences, and arrange conference travel.

steps.what: Lecturer scans journals and newsletters for developments in the field
Lecturer reads current literature
Lecturer talks with colleagues about developments
Lecturer prepares conference registration and travel: by e-mail today, in the university's travel portal after the change
Lecturer checks the final booking: conference, dates, travel and costs are right
Lecturer submits the checked booking in the travel portal
Lecturer participates in professional conferences

tasks.design: Journal content alerts and saved searches in the citation database send new papers on the lecturer's topics, so journals are not browsed one by one. Conference registration and travel go through the university's travel portal, where the lecturer checks each booking and submits it once. Reading, talking with colleagues and attending conferences stay with the lecturer.
tasks.previous_blocker: Journals were browsed issue by issue and travel arranged by e-mail.
tasks.enabler_now: Citation databases send alerts on saved searches.
tasks.still_hard: Alerts flood the inbox if searches are broad.
tasks.human_edge: Hearing at a conference what has not yet been published.
tasks.altitude: Less browsing and travel mail; reading stays.

reach.learn: Whether new findings reach courses sooner.

evidence.claim: Scopus AI gives topic summaries and foundational papers.

assumptions: Boundary: from field developments to the conference attended; teaching changes are outside.
Input contract: database licence held; fallback is browsing.
Reading and meeting colleagues do not change.
Travel approval rules do not change.
research_questions: Does time spent finding papers fall?

approvals.approved_version: The conference registration and travel booking with dates and costs exactly as checked by the lecturer in s4b, submitted once in the travel portal; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: alerts miss key journals, so browsing goes on and s1 keeps 85 (4.0); high: alerts cover the field as assumed (9.0).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The lecturer keeps designing assignments, researching, setting grades and keeping up with the field; retyped syllabi, hand marking and double grade entry shrink.
role.ambitious_version: A lecturer with more time for students and research.
